learning_goals: Explain what an LLM is and its three main limits
Define RAG and explain the meaning of Retrieval, Augmented, and Generation
Describe the three question-time steps in correct order: retrieve, augment, generate
List two benefits and one limitation of RAG

analogy.story: Imagine a student, Rohan, preparing for a government job exam. In a closed-book test, he answers only from memory — he might forget dates or make up facts. In an open-book test, he first searches the guide book for the right page (Retrieval), keeps that page open beside him (Augmented), and then writes the answer looking at that page (Generation).
analogy.mapping: Rohan's memory = LLM training data (fixed, cutoff). Guide book = External knowledge base (documents). Searching the right page = Retrieval (semantic search). Keeping page open = Augmentation (adding to prompt). Writing answer = Generation (LLM produces answer).

worked_example.setting: Priya, a 12th-pass student from Bhopal, uses a college chatbot on her phone to ask about a scholarship.
worked_example.question: What is the last date to apply for the Merit Scholarship 2024 at Bhopal Engineering College?
documents: Doc 1: Bhopal Engineering College Prospectus 2024. Merit Scholarship: Amount ₹20,000 per year. Eligibility: 85% in 12th. Application opens 1 June 2024. Last date to apply: 31 July 2024.
Doc 2: Hostel Fee Structure 2024. Boys hostel: ₹60,000/year. Girls hostel: ₹55,000/year. Mess charges extra.
Doc 3: Placement Stats 2023. Highest package ₹18 LPA. Average ₹6 LPA. Top recruiters: TCS, Infosys, Wipro.
worked_example.retrieved: Doc 1 snippet: 'Merit Scholarship: Amount ₹20,000 per year. Eligibility: 85% in 12th. Application opens 1 June 2024. Last date to apply: 31 July 2024.'
worked_example.answer_without_rag: The last date for most college scholarships in India is usually 30 June or 15 July. You should check the website.
worked_example.answer_with_rag: According to the Bhopal Engineering College Prospectus 2024, the last date to apply for the Merit Scholarship 2024 is 31 July 2024. [Source: Doc 1]

sections.heading: What You Will Learn
sections.goal: Set clear expectations for the lesson
points: What an LLM is and its three limits (knowledge cutoff, no private data, hallucination) [F1, F2, F3, F4, K1]
Full form of RAG and meaning of each word [F5, F6, K2]
Three question-time steps: Retrieve → Augment → Generate [F8, K3]
How documents are prepared: chunks, embeddings, vector database [F7, K4]
Benefits: fresh/private data, fewer hallucinations, sources, no retraining [F11, K5]
Limitation: answer quality depends on retrieval quality [F12, K6]
RAG does not retrain the model (contrast with fine-tuning) [F9, F10, K7]

sections.heading: Before We Start: Some Basic Ideas
sections.goal: Introduce AI, LLM, and LLM limits in simple words
points: AI = computer program that can do tasks needing human-like thinking (e.g., Google search, UPI fraud detection).
LLM (Large Language Model) = AI model trained on huge text (books, websites). It predicts next token (word/part of word) to generate text [F1]. Examples: models behind ChatGPT, Gemini.
Limit 1 — Knowledge Cutoff: LLM training stops at a fixed date. It knows nothing after that [F2].
Limit 2 — No Private Data: LLM never saw your college fee list, company policy, or personal notes [F3].
Limit 3 — Hallucination: LLM can sound confident but give wrong or made-up answers [F4, K1].

sections.heading: What Is RAG?
sections.goal: Define RAG and explain each word in the full form
points: RAG = Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Term from 2020 paper by Patrick Lewis et al. (Meta) [F6].
Retrieval = Finding/fetching relevant pieces of information from an outside source [F5].
Augmented = Added to / made stronger. The retrieved text is added to the user question in the prompt [F5].
Generation = The LLM writes (generates) the answer using the question + retrieved context [F5].
Simple definition: Before answering, the system first searches your documents, adds the found text to the question, then the LLM answers [F5, K2].

sections.heading: Why Does RAG Matter?
sections.goal: Explain benefits of RAG for real-world use
points: Uses up-to-date information (no knowledge cutoff problem) [F11].
Uses private/organisation data (college prospectus, company policy) [F11, F3].
Reduces hallucinations (fewer made-up answers) — but does not remove them completely [F11, M2].
Answers can show sources (citations) so you can verify [F11, F8].
Cheaper and faster than retraining the model [F11].
Easy to update knowledge: just change documents, not the model [F11, F9].

sections.heading: How Does RAG Work?
sections.goal: Explain preparation (indexing) and question-time steps (retrieve, augment, generate)
points: Preparation (done once before questions arrive) [F7, K4]:
1. Collect documents (PDFs, web pages, notes).
2. Split into small pieces called 'chunks' (e.g., 1-2 paragraphs each).
3. Turn each chunk into an 'embedding' — a list of numbers that captures the meaning of the text (not encryption, not compression) [F7, M4].
4. Store embeddings in a 'vector database' for fast meaning-based search.
Question-time steps (every user question) [F8, K3]:
1. Retrieve: User question → embedding → semantic search (find chunks with closest meaning) → take top-k chunks [F8, M5].
2. Augment: Put retrieved chunks into prompt with question + instruction like 'Answer using only this information' [F8].
3. Generate: LLM writes answer from question + retrieved context. Can cite sources [F8].
RAG does NOT change model weights. To update knowledge, update documents, not model [F9, K7].
Fine-tuning = trains model further, changes weights, slower/costlier, used for style/behaviour [F10, K7, M1].

sections.heading: Example: College Scholarship Chatbot
sections.goal: Show a concrete Indian scenario with retrieved snippet and grounded answer
points: Setting: Priya (12th-pass, Bhopal) uses college chatbot on phone [Worked Example].
Question: 'What is the last date to apply for the Merit Scholarship 2024 at Bhopal Engineering College?' [Worked Example].
Knowledge base has 3 documents (prospectus, hostel fees, placements) [Worked Example].
Retrieve: Semantic search finds Doc 1 snippet with scholarship dates [Worked Example].
Augment: Snippet added to prompt with instruction 'Answer using only this information' [F8].
Generate: LLM answers '31 July 2024' and cites Doc 1 [Worked Example].
Without RAG: LLM might guess '30 June' (hallucination) [F4, Worked Example].
With RAG: Correct, sourced answer [F11, Worked Example].

sections.heading: Key Words to Remember
sections.goal: Provide a simple glossary of all technical terms
points: AI: Computer program that mimics human thinking.
LLM: Large Language Model — predicts next token to generate text.
Token: A word or part of a word (LLM works in tokens).
Knowledge Cutoff: Date when LLM training stopped.
Hallucination: Confident but wrong/made-up answer.
RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation.
Retrieval: Finding relevant chunks from knowledge base.
Augmented: Adding retrieved text to the prompt.
Generation: LLM writing the final answer.
Chunk: Small piece of a document (1-2 paragraphs).
Embedding: List of numbers representing meaning of text.
Vector Database: Storage for embeddings, enables meaning-based search.
Semantic Search: Search by meaning, not just keywords.
Context Window: Max text LLM can take in one prompt (limits chunks).
Fine-tuning: Training model further to change weights (different from RAG).

points.q: What are the three limits of a plain LLM?
points.a: 1) Knowledge cutoff (fixed date), 2) No private data, 3) Can hallucinate (make up answers).

points.q: What does RAG stand for? Explain each word in one sentence.
points.a: Retrieval = find relevant chunks. Augmented = add chunks to prompt. Generation = LLM writes answer using them.

points.q: What is the correct order of steps when a user asks a question in RAG?
Does RAG retrain or change the LLM model?
points.a: No. RAG does not change model weights. To update knowledge, you update the documents only.

points.q: If the retrieval step returns a wrong or outdated chunk, what happens to the answer?
points.a: The answer can be wrong because RAG answer quality depends on retrieval quality.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.goal: Recap the whole lesson in 5 bullet points
points: LLM = predicts next token; limits: cutoff date, no private data, hallucination.
RAG = Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Before answering, system retrieves relevant chunks, adds them to prompt, then LLM generates.
Preparation: documents → chunks → embeddings → vector database (done once).
Question-time: Retrieve (semantic search) → Augment (add to prompt) → Generate (answer with citations).
Benefits: fresh/private data, fewer hallucinations, sources, no retraining. Limitation: answer only as good as retrieved chunks. RAG ≠ fine-tuning.
